detailed_rationale:
Infosys closed FY26 (year ended Mar-2026) with revenue crossing $20.2 billion, but the headline masks a currency mirage worth flagging up front: constant-currency (CC) growth was just 3.1% for the year, while INR-reported growth (the 9.6% figure in our quant snapshot) is inflated by rupee depreciation -- the real underlying growth rate the business is compounding at is the CC number, not the INR one. Q4 FY26 (Jan-Mar 2026) revenue was Rs 46,402 crore (+13.4% YoY reported), but CC revenue actually declined 1.3% sequentially -- a real deceleration heading into what is seasonally Infosys's weakest quarter. Net profit of Rs 8,501 crore (+20.9% YoY) was helped by a Rs 774 crore one-time tax-provision reversal, while operating margin held at 20.9% (Q4) / 21.0% (FY26 full year), management crediting the 'Project Maximus' efficiency program for absorbing wage hikes and AI-investment costs without margin slippage. Large-deal TCV for FY26 was $14.9 billion with a healthy 55% net-new mix (i.e., genuinely new scope, not renewals dressed up as wins) -- a real positive on deal quality. FY27 guidance, given alongside FY26 results on Apr-23-2026, is 1.5%-3.5% CC revenue growth and 20%-22% operating margin; the low end of that band is a genuine signal of caution, not sandbagging -- management's own language on the GenAI pricing debate is candid: AI is now 'compressing the existing book of business,' with some of that attributable to competitive intensity and pricing in a low-demand environment, on top of enterprises staying cautious on discretionary spend.

On earnings quality, there are two offsetting one-offs in FY26, not one: a Rs 1,289 crore exceptional provision (gratuity/leave liability from the new Labour Codes notified Nov-2025 -- the same item that hit L&T and other large India Inc names this cycle) was a genuine cost, but it was almost fully offset in the same year by the Rs 774 crore tax-provision reversal noted above -- net drag of roughly Rs 515 crore, immaterial (under 2% of FY26 PAT) at this scale, so headline PAT growth is a reasonably clean read of underlying profitability, not meaningfully flattered. No fresh McCamish-related cyber provision surfaced in FY26 -- Infosys filed a Dec-2025 6-K update on the McCamish cybersecurity incident with no new operational/financial detail disclosed, and the 2023 breach's US class-action settlement ($17.5 million) is already provided for and immaterial to a company of this scale. The more consequential and still-unresolved US policy risk is the $100,000-per-petition H-1B fee under the late-2025 US proclamation: Infosys has the highest exposure among Indian IT majors (over 93% of its FY2020-24 new H-1B hires, ~10,400 workers, were consulate-processed), and a naive replay of that hiring pattern at the new fee would run over $1 billion -- but the realistic FY27 hit is far smaller because firms will react (offshoring more delivery, cutting fresh H-1B filings, routing premium roles through L-1/GC-holders), and Infosys has not yet quantified a specific P&L number in its filings, only flagged the risk generically. Headcount fell 8,440 sequentially to 328,594 with attrition ticking up to 12.6% LTM -- both cyclical-normal, not red-flag moves, and the company still plans to hire ~20,000 freshers in FY27.

On the drawdown itself: the stock is down roughly 30-35% from its Feb-2026 high (~Rs 1,720 to ~Rs 1,100-1,124), which tracks closely with the Nifty IT index's ~29% YTD decline -- this reads as a sector-wide de-rating (Accenture's cautious FY26 guidance, weak US tech sentiment and IBM AI-linked commentary triggered a broad Indian-IT selloff in June 2026 that hit TCS, HCLTech and Wipro in the same window), not an Infosys-specific breakdown. At the current price, trailing P/E of ~14.9x sits about 34% below Infosys's own 10-year median (~22.7x) and below the IT-services peer median (~20.6x); FCF yield is ~4% against a 31.7% ROE, 41.4% ROCE, near-zero net leverage (D/E 0.1, interest cover 101.6x) and an actively executed capital-return policy -- Rs 37,500 crore returned to shareholders in FY26 via dividends plus the Rs 18,000 crore buyback completed Dec-2025 at Rs 1,800/share (about 39% above today's quote -- a useful, if imperfect, data point on where the company itself saw intrinsic value eighteen months ago). Q1 FY27 results are due July 23, 2026 (not yet out as of this review, five trading days out) -- Street models roughly Rs 41,000-41,875 crore revenue and 20.5%-21.5% operating margin, i.e., a soft, seasonally typical print, with the real signal being whether management reaffirms or trims the FY27 CC-growth band.
recommendation_rationale: Hold. The quant model already reads Hold across all three horizons (1y/3y/final) with the highest quality-score percentile in this coverage set (95.7) and zero balance-sheet red flags (GREEN) -- fundamentally this is not a broken business. Our own reverse-DCF read: at ~14.9x trailing earnings and a ~4% FCF yield, using an ~11% required equity return appropriate for a rupee large-cap compounder, the market is pricing roughly 6.5-7% perpetual per-share cash-flow growth (required-return minus FCF yield) -- almost exactly Infosys's own trailing 3-year revenue CAGR (6.8%) and only modestly above FY26's actual 3.1% CC growth. In plain terms: the ~30% drawdown has re-rated Infosys down to 'no credit for AI-led acceleration, no re-rating premium for the buyback/dividend engine' -- but it has NOT yet priced in permanent structural decline of the services model. That is a defensible, roughly fair-value resting point given genuine near-term guidance caution (1.5%-3.5% FY27 CC growth), not an obvious bargain and not a value trap either. Combined with a pristine, near-debt-free balance sheet, a steady $14.9 billion large-deal TCV book with a healthy 55% net-new mix, an intact ~85%-of-FCF capital-return policy, and no earnings-quality red flags once the two FY26 one-offs are netted against each other, there is no fundamental trigger here to sell into the drawdown. The case for adding fresh capital (not what this review is asked to judge) would need to wait for the July 23 print to show the FY27 guidance band is holding or improving; the case to hold the existing position does not depend on that.
summary: Infosys enters FY27 with FY26 revenue past $20 billion but real (constant-currency) growth of only 3.1%, a Rs 8,501 crore Q4 net profit partly aided by a one-time tax reversal that roughly offsets a separate Labour Code exceptional cost, a steady $14.9 billion large-deal book (55% net-new), and FY27 guidance cut to a cautious 1.5%-3.5% CC growth band reflecting genuine GenAI-driven pricing pressure on the existing book, not just conservatism. The stock's ~30-35% drawdown from Feb-2026 highs tracks the sector (Nifty IT -29% YTD) rather than an Infosys-specific breakdown, leaving it at ~14.9x trailing earnings (34% below its own 10-year median) with a pristine, near-debt-free balance sheet, 31.7% ROE and an active ~85%-of-FCF capital-return policy. Our reverse-DCF read is that the current price embeds roughly 6.5-7% perpetual per-share growth -- close to Infosys's own recent trend, not a doomsday assumption -- which argues the de-rating is largely sector-wide multiple compression rather than a fundamental breakdown. Hold: no balance-sheet, earnings-quality, or deal-pipeline red flag to justify selling, but also no valuation gap wide enough (nor mandate, in an existing-holdings review) to call this undervalued enough to add.
positive_para: FY26 revenue crossed $20.2 billion with a healthy $14.9 billion in large-deal TCV carrying a 55% net-new mix -- genuine fresh scope, not renewal relabeling -- and operating margin held at 21% for the full year despite wage-cycle and AI-investment cost pressure, credited to the Project Maximus efficiency program. The balance sheet is essentially pristine: D/E of 0.1, interest coverage of 101.6x, ROE of 31.7% and ROCE of 41.4%, with zero balance-sheet red flags (GREEN flag, quant quality-score percentile 95.7 -- the strongest in this coverage batch). Capital return is real and executed, not promised: Rs 37,500 crore returned to shareholders in FY26 via dividends (Rs 48/share total FY26 payout) plus a Rs 18,000 crore buyback completed Dec-2025 (10 crore shares extinguished at Rs 1,800/share), under an explicit policy of returning ~85% of cumulative 5-year FCF. At ~14.9x trailing earnings the stock sits 34% below its own 10-year median P/E (~22.7x) and below the IT-services peer median (~20.6x), and the ~30% YTD drawdown is substantially a sector-wide re-rating (Nifty IT -29% YTD, TCS/HCLTech/Wipro all down in the same June-2026 selloff triggered by Accenture's cautious guidance and US tech-sentiment weakness) rather than an Infosys-specific fundamental break. Our own reverse-DCF read finds the current price embeds only ~6.5-7% perpetual per-share growth -- close to Infosys's own trailing 3-year trend -- so the market is not obviously mispricing a healthy, well-capitalized compounder.
negative_para: FY27 guidance of 1.5%-3.5% CC revenue growth is genuinely cautious, not sandbagged -- Q4 FY26 CC revenue actually fell 1.3% sequentially, and management's own language acknowledges GenAI is 'compressing the existing book of business' via competitive pricing pressure in a low-demand environment, which is the core structural debate for the whole sector, not a company-specific issue Infosys can out-execute alone. FY26 earnings quality carries two offsetting one-offs -- a Rs 1,289 crore Labour Code exceptional provision largely offset by a Rs 774 crore tax-provision reversal -- that a mechanical PAT-growth read would not separate out. US policy risk is real and still unresolved: Infosys carries the highest H-1B exposure among Indian IT majors (over 93% of FY2020-24 new hires were consulate-processed), and the new $100,000-per-petition fee is a potential multi-hundred-million-dollar medium-term cost/margin risk that the company has flagged in filings but not yet quantified in guidance -- a live tail risk into FY27-28. Headcount fell 8,440 sequentially and attrition ticked up to 12.6% LTM, both unremarkable on their own but consistent with a company managing through a soft demand patch rather than one in expansion mode. Finally, Q1 FY27 results (July 23, 2026) are a real near-term event-risk window: Street models a soft, seasonally typical print, and any further trim to the already-wide 1.5%-3.5% FY27 band would be a legitimate reason to revisit this Hold.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~14.9x trailing earnings and a ~4% FCF yield, and using an ~11% required equity return appropriate for a large-cap rupee compounder (roughly a 6.5-7% risk-free G-sec yield plus a modest equity risk premium), the implied perpetual per-share cash-flow growth priced into Infosys today is roughly 6.5-7% (required return minus FCF yield) -- essentially identical to Infosys's own trailing 3-year revenue CAGR of 6.8%, and only modestly above FY26's actual 3.1% CC growth. That is the key judgment call: the market is NOT pricing a structural collapse of the IT-services model (that would show up as a mid-single-digit or negative implied growth rate, or a FCF yield well above 6-7%); it is pricing continuation of Infosys's recent trend with zero credit for AI-led re-acceleration and zero re-rating premium for the buyback/dividend engine. Given Infosys is guiding FY27 CC growth of only 1.5%-3.5% (below the growth rate the market is implicitly demanding), the stock is arguably priced for a modest recovery in FY28-29 as large-deal ramp and eventual discretionary-spend normalization offset the near-term GenAI pricing drag -- a plausible, not heroic, assumption for a company with a $14.9 billion, 55%-net-new deal book and no balance-sheet constraint on executing it. This is a fair-value-to-mildly-cheap read, not a screaming bargain (there is no wide margin of safety if FY27 guidance gets cut further at the July 23 print or beyond) and not a value trap (the implied growth ask is below, not above, Infosys's own demonstrated trend) -- consistent with Hold rather than a valuation-driven Sell.
